newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Belgrade lawyers block courts in tax protest.
newsitem.headline: Belgrade lawyers block courts in tax protest.

text.p: Belgrade lawyers paralysed city courts on Friday to protest high taxes they say few can afford to pay.
"Our intention is to block the courts for a week by not appearing before them or any other institutions," Radoslav Nedic, president of the Belgrade Bar Association told Reuters.

He said the Bar Association, representing more than 50 percent of Serbia's lawyers, met on Monday and decided to launch a seven-day protest beginning on Friday over high taxes and an increasingly troubled judicial system.
"Such exorbitant taxes have driven many of my collegues to the edge of survival," Nedic said. "About 70 percent of lawyers simply cannot afford to pay them."
Nedic said the action was a protest and not a strike, because Serbian law prohibits lawyers from striking.
The state-controlled newspaper Politika said on Friday the lawyers' protest was groundless because authorities had already cancelled penalties on unpaid taxes.
"It is the maximum the state could do to ease the burden for the economy and private businesses," the paper said.
The lawyers were demanding a simpler tax system which would correspond to the real purchasing power of taxpayers and current economic conditions.
Nikola Vavic, who has been practising law for two years, accused the state of setting enormous taxes without any regard for the poor state of the economy.
Vavic said he works 14-15 hours a day and has to pay two-thirds of his gross income in taxes, taking home only about 1,180 dinars ($236) per month.
"The state doesn't recognise any of my costs, but they are prepared to seize my assets if I cannot pay taxes regularly."
The Belgrade city court looked mostly empty on Friday morning as all cases requiring the presence of a lawyer were postponed.
Ivan Bajazit, a judge in the Belgrade district court, said all trials scheduled for the following week would be delayed.
"I understand their (lawyers) problems. But clients will be more hit by the protest than the state itself," he said.
